Volume 16 · Chapter 11

Seminars, revision and oral defense

Research Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v16-c10

By the endDefend research under probing questions and revise based on justified criticism.

A seminar tests whether an argument survives contact with another person's reasoning. A defense succeeds when the speaker can locate a claim's support, change the conclusion when an assumption changes, and identify what remains unknown. Fluency alone does none of these things.

Capability: present a research argument, answer probing questions, turn justified criticism into traceable revisions, and disagree without confusing confidence with evidence. Prerequisite: Chapter 10's complete-paper architecture. Chapter 4 supplies the referee's perspective; here the researcher must actually respond. The two fictional artifacts below use original synthetic data. Neither is an empirical discovery or a record of a learner's performance.

1. Give the audience an argument it can inspect

A claim says what follows; its warrant connects evidence and assumptions to that conclusion. A revision changes the research artifact, while a response memo tells the reader where and why it changed. A defense tests the speaker's command of both, including unfamiliar objections. Distinguish a descriptive contrast, a causal estimand, an economic mechanism and a policy recommendation before writing the opening sentence. Moving between them requires additional support, not a more persuasive slide.

Build a talk around a question, the smallest evidence sufficient to understand the answer, the decisive inferential step and the scope of the conclusion. Introduce units and notation before displaying a result. Put the central limitation next to the result it qualifies. Reserve appendices for details that a listener can request; do not hide an assumption necessary to understand the headline there. Board and Meyer-ter-Vehn's discussion of economic purpose, explicit primitives and the distinction between results and interpretation motivates this architecture, although their guide concerns theory papers rather than a tested seminar protocol.[1]

Write a speaking script once to discover missing transitions. Then rehearse from a compact argument map: question → object → evidence → warrant → conclusion. Time an actual rehearsal, including pointing to figures and allowing silence after the main result. If it overruns, remove secondary material before accelerating delivery. The timings below are a proposed allocation, not an observed rehearsal. They include deliberate pauses; a speaker must measure and adjust their own pace.

For questions, first establish what is being challenged: arithmetic, measurement, identification, mechanism, relevance, or presentation. Give the answer in the first sentence; then supply the decisive reason and its consequence. If the premise is unclear, restate it and ask whether that is the intended question. If you do not know, specify what you do know, what information is missing and how it would change the answer. Do not substitute an unrelated prepared speech. If an interruption requires a long derivation, state the short answer now and offer the derivation after the central argument, subject to the chair's time allocation.

2. Worked artifact: a complete ten-minute research talk

Title: “A lending contrast and its missing counterfactual.” Audience: economists who know potential outcomes but have not seen this example. Format: a proposed ten-minute presentation followed by a separate question period. Five speaking segments receive (2, 2, 3, 2, 1) minutes, totaling 10. The script below is the complete main talk; the table and equation are its two visual aids.

Visual aid A: all the observations

The invented event occurs between dates 0 and 1. “Exposed” means designated exposure before the event, not randomized treatment. Loan stocks are millions of one currency, measured at both dates within the same bank reporting perimeter. No entries, exits, revaluations or classification changes occur in this constructed example. Banks have equal weight.

Original synthetic bank loan stocks
BankGroupDate 0Date 1
AExposed4036
BExposed6054
CComparator5050
DComparator5052

0–2 minutes: question and contribution

“When banks exposed to a funding event reduce lending relative to other banks, what have we learned? I will separate the observed lending contrast from the causal effect of exposure. That distinction matters because a policy restoring funding would be justified by a claim about what would happen under intervention, not simply by a comparison of recorded balances.

“This is a deliberately small synthetic example. Its contribution is to make an identification gap visible; it is not evidence about an actual banking episode. Everything observed fits in this table. At date zero, the two exposed banks have loan stocks of forty and sixty million. At date one they have thirty-six and fifty-four. The comparator banks begin at fifty each and end at fifty and fifty-two. Exposure was designated before the event, but designation alone does not make the groups exchangeable.

“I will show the contrast, construct two explanations that produce exactly these observations, and then state what an explicit restriction on the missing counterfactual would buy us. Please keep one question in mind: what would exposed banks have done without exposure?”

2–4 minutes: measurement and result

“These are stocks of loans, not new originations, borrower spending or welfare. Their measurement perimeter is fixed by construction. Each bank receives equal weight. The exposed mean falls from fifty to forty-five million. The comparator mean rises from fifty to fifty-one. Changes are therefore minus five and plus one million; subtracting the latter from the former gives minus six million.

“The exposed group's observed proportional change is minus ten percent. A different quantity, the minus-six contrast divided by the common fifty-million baseline, is minus twelve percent. I will call that a baseline-normalized contrast, not a twelve-percent causal effect. Equal baseline means make that normalization easy here; they do not establish that untreated trends would have been equal.

“There are only four constructed banks and no sampling design in this demonstration. I am not presenting a population confidence interval. Reproducing the subtraction would verify the calculation but leave the causal question open. The next visual makes the missing assumption explicit.”

4–7 minutes: warrant and counterexample

Visual aid B: D = τ + b. Here D is the observed difference in mean changes; τ is the mean date-1 causal effect of exposure on the exposed banks; and b is the difference between the exposed banks' untreated trend and the comparator banks' observed trend. All three use millions per bank. For this interpretation, assume no anticipation at date 0 and that comparator outcomes represent their untreated outcomes, including no spillovers from the exposed banks.

“To see the identity, add and subtract the exposed banks' mean date-one outcome without exposure. The exposed observed change becomes its untreated change plus its treatment effect. Subtracting the comparator change leaves the treatment effect plus the untreated-trend difference. The equation is an accounting decomposition of potential outcomes under the stated setup, not a reason for setting the second term to zero.

“Consider a first possible world. Without exposure, A would have ended at forty-one and B at sixty-one million. Their mean would be fifty-one, matching the comparators' mean increase of one. The exposed treatment effect is then forty-five minus fifty-one, or minus six; b is zero. In a second world, their untreated outcomes would be thirty-six and fifty-four. The mean would already have fallen to forty-five without exposure. Treatment has zero effect and b equals minus six. Both worlds generate every observed cell in the table. I cannot use the table to choose between them.

“This does not prove that the event had no effect. It proves that these observations and the stated setup do not select one effect. The same relative decline could reflect exposure, different borrower demand trends, or other factors contained in the missing untreated path. Those are possibilities to investigate, not additional facts established by the table. Nor does a negative lending effect, even if identified, uniquely establish a liquidity mechanism. The transmission channel needs its own evidence.”

7–9 minutes: a conditional answer

“Suppose, as a sensitivity exercise, someone can defend that b lies between minus two and plus one million. Since τ equals minus six minus b, the compatible effect interval runs from minus seven to minus four million. The interval endpoints reverse the endpoints of b because increasing the untreated trend makes the effect more negative. These are conditional identification bounds, not sampling confidence limits.

“The displayed range is an assumption, not something learned from these four observations. Its usefulness depends on independent support for how different untreated trends could have been. Earlier comparable observations, institutional information and a defensible treatment-assignment argument could help assess that restriction; none has been supplied here. I would show readers how conclusions change under alternative restrictions instead of selecting a narrow range because it preserves the desired sign.

“Notice the result's scope. Even this negative conditional effect is per exposed bank. Other lenders could replace the lost loans, borrowers could change financing sources, and social costs and benefits could differ. An aggregate credit or welfare recommendation requires a different target and additional evidence.”

9–10 minutes: conclusion

“The descriptive answer is a minus-six-million difference in mean changes. The causal answer is conditional: with equal untreated trends it equals minus six; with the stated bounded trend difference it lies between minus seven and minus four; without such a restriction these observations do not determine its sign. My next research step is to investigate the treatment assignment and the untreated comparison, not merely enlarge the result table. A strong intervention claim would remain premature. The argument I ask you to evaluate today is narrower: this contrast is correctly measured within the constructed example, and the counterfactual assumption determines what it can mean.”

Calculation sheet available during questions

Bank changes: (-4, -6, 0, 2). Exposed means, before/after: (50, 45); comparator means: (50, 51). Group changes: (-5, 1); D = -6. Observed exposed growth = -1/10; baseline-normalized D = -3/25. World A untreated exposed outcomes (41, 61) yield (τ, b) = (-6, 0). World B (36, 54) yields (0, -6). Assumed b bounds (-2, 1) yield τ bounds (-7, -4).

A probing question period: complete responses

Question: “Your title avoids the important question. Did funding exposure cause the decline?”

“The table alone does not identify that effect. It gives D = −6, while the two constructed untreated paths produce effects −6 and 0 with identical observations. If equal untreated trends is defended, −6 becomes a causal estimate in this setup; I have not supplied that defense. I agree that the causal question is important, and the current artifact establishes a limit rather than answering it unconditionally.”

Question: “You said twelve percent. The exposed banks fell only ten percent. Is your arithmetic wrong?”

“Those are different quantities. The exposed mean fell by 5 from 50, giving −10%. The relative-change contrast is −6 divided by 50, giving −12%. Calling the latter the observed percentage fall would be wrong. I will keep the descriptive result in millions in the headline and name the denominator whenever I show the normalization.”

Question: “Why should I believe your interval for b?”

“You should not treat it as established by this example. I chose it to demonstrate conditional sensitivity. To use it substantively I would need an independent argument about untreated trends, including possible comparator spillovers and the assignment of exposure. Until then, the interval is an illustration; it is not a result validated by these data.”

Question: “Why not add more banks and solve the problem with a smaller standard error?”

“A larger appropriate sample could reduce sampling uncertainty, but it does not by itself restrict b. A population can preserve the same systematic untreated-trend difference. I would need to explain why the expanded comparison supports the counterfactual, and specify sampling and dependence before reporting uncertainty. More observations and identification repair are separate tasks.”

Question: “Suppose borrower demand fell at exposed banks. Is your funding mechanism disproved?”

“No. Demand differences are an alternative explanation, not a demonstrated fact here. They could explain all or part of the contrast. This table cannot distinguish a funding-supply channel from demand or other channels. A borrower-linked design or credible exogenous funding variation might help, but each would need its own assumptions and measurement. I cannot claim to have run that analysis.”

Question: “What share of these borrowers moved to another lender?”

“I do not know: the synthetic table contains no borrower links. Bank balance changes cannot answer that question. To target borrower credit I would need borrower-level exposures and borrowing across lenders, with matching and coverage documented. I will record it as an unresolved measurement requirement, not invent a substitution rate.”

Question: “Your failure to identify a negative effect means the true effect is zero.”

“That conclusion does not follow. Zero and −6 are both compatible with the observations, and other effects are possible under other untreated paths. Nonidentification is not evidence selecting the zero-effect world. We agree that I should remove an unconditional negative-effect claim; we should not replace it with an unconditional zero-effect claim.”

Post-seminar record: the percentage-language objection is resolved by explicit denominators in the script and calculation sheet. Credibility of the b range remains unresolved; it stays labeled illustrative. Borrower substitution is unanswered and requires new data. Assignment and spillover investigations are proposed work, not completed work. Preserve the question, your answer and its consequence while memory is fresh; do not convert a courteous audience into evidence of approval.

3. Revision is a change to the argument, not a letter-writing exercise

First reconstruct the strongest reasonable version of a criticism. Classify it by its consequence for the main claim: essential correction, evidence needed for a retained claim, optional extension, or misunderstanding caused by presentation. A presentation problem can still be consequential if the wording invites a false interpretation. Berk, Harvey and Hirshleifer distinguish supported major objections from optional requests and discuss proportionate follow-up; here we apply that distinction to the author's response.[2]

Choose explicitly among repairing support, narrowing the claim, or withdrawing it. “Beyond scope” cannot save a conclusion whose support requires the requested analysis. It can justify declining an extension once the manuscript no longer makes the claim that would require it. A new limitation sentence cannot repair an unchanged causal title, abstract and conclusion. Search all dependent claims and revise figures, captions, summary and policy discussion together.

A usable response has four parts: the concern, your judgment, the actual change or reason for declining, and a locator to the revised evidence. Mark a concern resolved only after inspecting the artifact. “We agree” without a change is unresolved; added analysis that still lacks its required assumption is partly addressed at most. When criticism reveals a fatal gap, preserve the failed claim in the change record, not as a disguised implication in the new conclusion. Disagreement should target an inference or request, not the critic's motives or status.

4. Worked artifact: revision dossier and oral defense

The fictional paper behind the talk originally overstated the same four-bank calculation. The author decides to offer a descriptive teaching note rather than pretend that new identification evidence exists. A venue requiring an identified causal contribution could still reject this narrower paper. Correcting validity does not establish novelty, importance or editorial fit.

Original submitted excerpt, version 0

“Funding exposure cuts lending by twelve percent. Exposed and comparison banks start at the same average lending, so the comparison isolates the effect. The decline demonstrates a liquidity mechanism. Restoring funding will increase aggregate credit and improve welfare.”

The subtraction was reproducible. Every inferential sentence after it exceeded the supplied support: equal baseline levels do not imply equal untreated changes; loan stocks do not isolate a mechanism; exposed-bank effects do not equal aggregate credit effects; and no welfare criterion or cost was specified.

Replacement title and abstract, version 1

Title: “A lending contrast and its missing counterfactual.”

Abstract: “This synthetic four-bank note shows a −6 million difference in mean loan-stock changes between exposed and comparator banks. The exposed mean itself falls by 10%; dividing the contrast by the common initial mean gives a distinct −12% normalization. Under no anticipation and unaffected comparators, the contrast equals the exposed effect plus the untreated-trend difference. Two counterfactual constructions produce the same observations with effects −6 and 0. An illustrative untreated-trend restriction yields conditional effect bounds, without a claim that the restriction is established. The example clarifies what evidence an intervention claim would require; it establishes neither a lending mechanism nor aggregate welfare consequences.”

Replacement measurement and identification paragraphs

“The unit is a bank. Outcomes are loan stocks in millions of one currency at two dates, with a fixed reporting perimeter and equal bank weights. The table contains the entire synthetic input. We report exposed and comparator means and their changes before the relative-change contrast. We distinguish the exposed group's own proportional change from a contrast normalized by its baseline. Neither is a measure of total borrower financing.”

“Let the exposed mean untreated date-1 stock be m. Its baseline mean is 50 and the comparator change is 1. Then b = (m − 50) − 1 = m − 51, while τ = 45 − m, giving D = τ + b = −6. This interpretation assumes no anticipation and unaffected comparators; the table supplies neither assumption. Every b in the illustrative interval [−2, 1] corresponds to m = 51 + b, hence m in [49, 52] and τ in [−7, −4]. The bounds are sharp within this constructed mean-outcome setup: setting A's untreated date-1 stock to m − 10 and B's to m + 10 attains each m while preserving observed outcomes and nonnegative stocks. These conditional bounds are not sampling intervals.”

Displayed endpoint witnesses: m = (49, 52); corresponding untreated (A, B) pairs ((39, 59), (42, 62)). No cross-world restriction links these unobserved outcomes to actual outcomes beyond the stated setup.

Replacement conclusion

“The observed relative decline is a descriptive fact of the constructed table. A causal interpretation depends on an untreated-trend restriction and the comparison setup. We therefore withdraw the mechanism and welfare conclusions. A substantive application would need evidence about assignment and untreated trends, and a borrower-level target would need linked financing information. This revision does not provide those inputs or establish a new empirical contribution.”

Complete response memo to three substantial comments

Opening: “Thank you for identifying the gap between our calculation and its interpretation. We agree that version 0 did not justify its causal, mechanism or welfare claims. Version 1 is now a descriptive instructional note. Below we distinguish completed textual and analytic repairs from evidence we do not possess. We recognize that the revised contribution may not meet a venue's original causal-research remit.”

Comment 1: “Equal initial means do not establish the counterfactual trend. Supply a credible design or remove the causal claim.” Response: “We accept the objection and choose the second remedy. The replacement title and abstract remove the causal headline. The identification paragraph defines the missing untreated-trend term, constructs both the −6 and zero-effect worlds, and labels sensitivity restrictions as assumptions. The replacement conclusion withdraws the mechanism and welfare statements. Locations: revised abstract, measurement/identification and conclusion. Verification: both worlds reproduce every observed cell. This resolves the overclaim by narrowing the paper; it does not resolve causal identification.”

Comment 2: “The twelve-percent statement confuses a percentage change with a normalized contrast; report units and construction.” Response: “We accept this correction. The exposed mean changes from 50 to 45, so its own proportional change is −10%. The −6 contrast divided by 50 is −12%; it is now explicitly named a baseline-normalized contrast. The complete input table, calculation sheet and replacement measurement paragraph state millions, equal weights and fixed perimeter. Locations: table, calculation sheet within the talk and measurement paragraph. Verification: recomputing group means yields −5 and +1 changes. The correction is complete for this synthetic example; real-data measurement quality is not claimed.”

Comment 3: “Estimate a dynamic general-equilibrium model in several countries before discussing aggregate credit and welfare.” Response: “We agree that the original aggregate and welfare claims required evidence absent from the submission. We have removed those claims throughout. We decline the proposed multi-country model as an extension of the revised descriptive teaching note, not because aggregate substitution or welfare costs are unimportant. The replacement conclusion now states those unresolved requirements. If the editorial objective remains a substantive policy paper, our narrower revision will not satisfy it. No new-country analysis or policy validation is claimed.”

Closing: “The changes above repair the mismatch between evidence and claims. The credibility of an untreated-trend restriction, empirical novelty and external applicability remain unestablished. We have not marked those research questions complete.”

Revision disposition checked against the revised text
ConcernActual artifact inspectedDisposition
Causal overclaimTitle, abstract, method and conclusionResolved by withdrawal; causal identification remains unresolved
Percentage and measurement ambiguityInput table, calculation sheet, measurement paragraphResolved within the synthetic example
Aggregate/welfare supportAbstract and conclusionClaims withdrawn; requested extension declined, not completed

Defense with an unfamiliar change in assumptions

Examiner: “Your central table remains unchanged, but allow b between −7 and 1. Derive the effect set now. Does your negative-sign conclusion survive? Show realizable endpoints rather than repeating a formula.”

Candidate: “No, the sign conclusion does not survive. Since τ = −6 − b decreases in b, its minimum is −7 at b = 1 and its maximum is 1 at b = −7. The effect set is [−7, 1]. At the lower b endpoint the exposed untreated mean is 44, realized by A = 34 and B = 54; observed exposed mean 45 then gives effect 1. At b = 1 the untreated mean is 52, realized by A = 42 and B = 62, giving effect −7. All these stocks are nonnegative and keep the actual table fixed. At b = −6, m = 45 and the effect is zero. I must remove any unconditional negative-sign sentence from the defense and report how the conclusion depends on the bound.”

Changed bounds (-7, 1); effect set (-7, 1); endpoint untreated means (44, 52); endpoint (A, B) pairs ((34, 54), (42, 62)); zero-effect b = -6.

Examiner: “Now change the target to total credit available to the banks' original borrowers. Can we double your per-bank effect?” Candidate: “No. Doubling would aggregate effects over the two exposed banks under that same bank-level target, not over their borrowers' credit from all sources. Borrowers can move across banks, hold multiple relationships or obtain nonbank finance. I need a defined borrower population, linked borrowing across sources and a counterfactual for total borrower credit. The current table cannot supply the new target. I would amend the research question and data plan before estimating it.”

Examiner: “Then why retain this paper?” Candidate: “It can be a transparent teaching demonstration of a contrast and its missing counterfactual. I cannot defend it as a novel causal banking result. Whether that instructional contribution merits this venue is a separate judgment. If the required contribution is causal evidence, I should pursue an adequate design or withdraw from that venue, not restore the old headline.”

An assessment protocol that requires real evidence

Before a real session, give an independent examiner the current paper, prior version, response memo and executable calculations. Ask for the timed talk, questions about its weakest link, and at least one unseen change in assumptions or target. The examiner records the actual question, the candidate's unedited answer, follow-up prompts, time taken and the resulting judgment. Keep “not observed” distinct from “incorrect.” A rehearsed script is preparation; it cannot fill an observation record.

Assess four domains separately: (1) accurate reconstruction of results, units and assumptions; (2) justified claim boundaries and alternative explanations; (3) reasoning under changed assumptions; (4) traceable revision and substantive engagement with disagreement. For each, record evidence as independent performance, performance after a prompt, or not yet demonstrated. Advancement in this author-designed protocol requires independent performance in all four, plus correction of any material false claim. Clear speech helps the examiner inspect reasoning but does not compensate for an identification error. These are instructional criteria, not institutional qualification rules.

If a learner cannot solve the changed-bound defense, the remediation is to derive D = τ + b, construct endpoint worlds and practice on a different interval. Reassessment uses a new interval or target and records a new unprompted response. A passing arithmetic answer with an unsupported claim that the bound is empirically verified still fails the claim-boundary domain. External human judgment of the learner and the research remains necessary; no performance has been observed in this chapter.

5. Exercises

For open responses, assess the stated claim, evidence, assumptions and consequence, not agreement with a preferred policy. Use the complete synthetic table and no imagined additional data.

  1. Replace “Exposure cuts bank lending twelve percent, proving a liquidity channel” with a seminar opening of at most three sentences. State the descriptive result, the question and the missing support.
  2. Recompute both groups' baseline and final means, both changes, D, exposed growth and baseline-normalized D. Explain exactly why the last two numbers differ and why neither calculation alone validates a causal claim.
  3. An audience member says that equal baseline group means prove parallel untreated trends. Give a complete reply using both counterfactual worlds from the talk. Show each world's exposed untreated mean, b and τ, and say what is and is not refuted.
  4. The discussant asks where [−2, 1] for b comes from and whether it is a 95% confidence interval. Give a direct answer, derive the compatible effect set, exhibit attainable endpoints and identify what evidence is still missing.
  5. A referee demands a credible causal design or removal of the causal headline, then requests a multi-country policy model. You possess only the table. Write a response to both demands, including actual replacement conclusion text and a precise statement of what is unresolved.
  6. Without consulting the scripted defense, derive the effect set under b ∈ [−7, 1], its zero-effect value and realizable endpoint outcomes. Then explain why doubling a per-bank effect does not answer the total-borrower-credit question.
  7. A critic concludes that nonidentification proves a zero effect and calls refusal to estimate more countries evasive. Write a principled disagreement that concedes the justified point, rejects the invalid inference and makes clear when declining the extension would be indefensible.
  8. In a real mock defense, the candidate independently computes D but gives [−7, −4] after the examiner widens b to [−7, 1]. After a prompt the candidate corrects it to [−7, 1], then says the bound has been empirically validated. The memo accurately removes all causal and welfare claims. Produce a four-domain assessment record, a remediation task and an unseen reassessment. Do not mark unobserved work complete.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

1. Opening with a defensible target

“In this synthetic four-bank table, exposed banks' mean loan-stock change is 6 million below the comparator change. Does that relative decline represent the effect of exposure? Answering causally requires a defensible untreated comparison, and identifying a liquidity channel requires additional evidence beyond the balance changes.” This states the result, motivates the causal question and identifies two different gaps. A good alternative may include the −12% normalization if it names its denominator and never calls it the exposed group's own decline or a proved effect.

2. Complete calculation

Exposed baseline (40 + 60)/2 = 50 and final (36 + 54)/2 = 45; comparator baseline (50 + 50)/2 = 50 and final (50 + 52)/2 = 51. Changes are 45 − 50 = −5 and 51 − 50 = 1. Thus D = −5 − 1 = −6 million per bank. Exposed growth is (45 − 50)/50 = −1/10 = −10%. Normalized D is −6/50 = −3/25 = −12%. Their two-percentage-point difference reflects subtracting the comparator's +1/50 = +2% change. These are equal-weight group calculations with a common baseline here. Neither supplies the missing untreated exposed trend; correct arithmetic is compatible with either counterfactual world.

3. Equal levels do not select trends

“Equal starting means tell us both groups begin at 50; they say nothing about the unobserved exposed trend without the event. If untreated A and B end at 41 and 61, their mean is 51, so b = (51 − 50) − 1 = 0 and τ = 45 − 51 = −6. If they instead end at 36 and 54, their mean is 45, so b = (45 − 50) − 1 = −6 and τ = 45 − 45 = 0. Both retain every observed input. This refutes the claim that equal baseline means imply equal untreated trends; it does not establish which world actually applies.” Full credit requires the two observationally equivalent constructions and that last distinction, not just the word “endogeneity.”

4. An assumption is not a confidence level

“The interval is illustrative and is not estimated from these data or calibrated to 95% coverage. Under that restriction, τ = −6 − b is decreasing, so b = 1 gives −7 and b = −2 gives −4. At b = −2, m = 49 and untreated outcomes (39, 59) attain τ = −4. At b = 1, m = 52 and (42, 62) attain τ = −7. Every intermediate m is attained by (m − 10, m + 10), preserving nonnegative stocks. Thus the conditional identified set is exactly [−7, −4] under the setup. Independent support for the untreated-trend restriction, no anticipation and unaffected comparators is still missing. A sampling confidence procedure would be a separate task requiring a sampling model.” Evaluation requires direct acknowledgment of the source gap; a polished derivation with invented validation is insufficient.

5. A consequential response, with changed text

“We accept that the causal headline lacks a credible design. We remove it from the title, abstract and conclusion and add the two compatible counterfactual worlds in the identification section. Our replacement conclusion reads: ‘The synthetic table shows a −6 million difference in mean loan-stock changes. This contrast does not by itself identify an exposure effect or mechanism. Causal analysis requires a defensible untreated comparison; aggregate and welfare claims require further targets and evidence that this note does not supply.’ We decline the multi-country policy model for this narrowed descriptive note and withdraw the claims it was requested to support. If the venue requires a causal policy contribution, this revision is not sufficient for that objective.” The response resolves the unsupported claim, not identification or novelty. Credit requires an actual replacement paragraph, affected locations and honest unresolved status; merely saying “beyond scope” while retaining the old conclusion fails.

6. Transfer under a changed bound and target

Since D = −6, subtracting b ∈ [−7, 1] gives τ ∈ [−6 − 1, −6 − (−7)] = [−7, 1]. Zero requires b = −6, which is inside the interval. At b = −7, m = 44 and untreated (34, 54) yield τ = 1. At b = 1, m = 52 and untreated (42, 62) yield τ = −7. The same construction covers all intermediate values. Hence a negative sign is no longer identified. Twice a per-bank mean effect would target the total at the two exposed banks under that setup. Original borrowers' total credit also includes other banks and nonbank sources, may involve overlapping relationships and requires an identified borrower population and its counterfactual. The table cannot provide it.

7. Disagreement with concessions and boundaries

“I agree that our table cannot justify the original causal policy headline, and we have withdrawn it. I disagree that this selects a zero effect: the worlds with effects −6 and 0 both match every observation. More countries might provide useful variation, but their number alone would not validate a counterfactual. We decline a multi-country policy model for the revised descriptive demonstration while acknowledging that it does not answer the policy question. Declining required policy analysis would be indefensible if we retained the policy conclusion, or represented this narrowed note as satisfying a venue's requirement for causal policy evidence.” Evaluate the inference and the resulting manuscript scope, not the critic's tone. An answer that attacks the critic, claims zero is disproved, or treats workload as a warrant for the original claims is inadequate.

8. An evidence-based assessment record

Results/units/assumptions: D was computed independently, but the record does not establish the full domain: units and all setup assumptions were not reported as tested. Record independent performance on D and “not yet demonstrated” for the remainder. Claim boundaries: not yet demonstrated; the unsupported assertion of empirical validation is a material error. Changed assumptions: performance after a prompt, not independent; the initial interval was wrong for the new bound. Traceable revision/disagreement: the memo's actual claim withdrawals are evidenced; substantive handling of disagreement was not observed, so the full domain remains not yet demonstrated. Do not advance under the protocol.

Remediation: derive the decreasing map τ = D − b, draw the endpoints, construct compatible outcomes, and label separately observed facts, maintained setup assumptions and hypothetical restrictions. Correct the false validation statement in a written response. Reassess unprompted with b ∈ (-4, 2): τ ∈ (−8, −2), using m ∈ (47, 53) and untreated pairs ((37, 57), (43, 63)). Then ask whether this proves a liquidity channel and why the bound should be believed. The mathematical interval is negative; neither the channel nor the restriction's credibility follows. Record the actual new answers, including units, setup assumptions and disagreement handling, before deciding. The reassessment described here has not been administered.

6. Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back: explain to a colleague why a successful revision can repair a paper without answering its original causal question. Use the two worlds and one sentence from the replacement conclusion. Answer guide: both worlds preserve the table while changing τ, so the data did not acquire identifying power. The revision succeeds by removing unsupported inferences and accurately stating the remaining descriptive contribution. It may still fail a venue's substantive contribution standard.

After a delay, without the script: reconstruct D = τ + b, explain what changes when the allowed b interval widens, and write the first two sentences of an answer to an unknown borrower-substitution question. Answer guide: add and subtract the exposed untreated date-1 mean; a larger b set creates a weakly larger compatible effect set and may cross zero. “The table has no borrower links, so I do not know the substitution share. To answer, I need linked borrowing across sources for a defined borrower population and a credible counterfactual.” A genuine retention check records the learner's answer before opening this guide.

For deeper work, rehearse with an independent field expert using the actual paper, not only this example. Ask for an unfamiliar assumption change and revise the manuscript afterward. Preserve the question log, version comparison and evidence of follow-up. Chapter 12 turns these artifacts into a research agenda; their existence alone does not demonstrate an original contribution or a successful real defense.

Sources and further study

  • Simon Board and Moritz Meyer-ter-Vehn, Writing Economic Theory Papers — A stated economic question, transparent model primitives and qualified contribution; separating theorem, proof and interpretation. Used in original C12 critique and writing instruction; not evidence for the new models.
  • Jonathan B. Berk, Campbell R. Harvey and David Hirshleifer, Preparing a Referee Report: Guidelines and Perspectives — A referee’s concise contribution summary, evidence for consequential objections, distinction between required repair and optional extension, and proportionate follow-up. Used in original C12 critique and writing instruction; not evidence for the new models.
